subjects.introduction: Every religion has had to ask what happens when the people who loved its founder cannot agree on who speaks for him afterward. Bahá’u’lláh answered that question in writing before He died, and the question of fidelity to that written Covenant runs through everything here: the appointment of a Centre, the promise that unity would be preserved, and the sorrow of ‘Abdu’l‑Bahá when brothers and old companions turned against it for the sake of leadership, as Judas once turned for a few pieces of silver. The opposition is pictured as foam on an ocean that soon disperses, as a rootless tree, as a disease that spreads if not kept at a distance. Yet the same voice that commands avoidance forbids violence, harsh speech and vengeance, distinguishes weakness from deliberate malice, prays for those who have strayed, and keeps the door of repentance open. To read this is to be drawn toward what firmness in the Covenant asks of a single life, toward the discipline of defending the Faith without cruelty, and toward the grief and prayer through which unity is finally preserved.
